name: Prairie View A&M University
affiliation: State of Texas (Texas A&M University System); 1890 land-grant
formerNames: Alta Vista Agricultural and Mechanical College of Texas for Colored Youth
Prairie View State Normal & Industrial College
Prairie View A&M College of Texas
description: Authorized by the Texas Legislature in 1876 as the Black branch of the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Texas, Prairie View opened in 1878 as Alta Vista Agricultural College with eight students. It became Texas' second-oldest public university and a pipeline of Black teachers, engineers and military officers. Its MBA program produced oil executive Kase Lawal, and its engineering school produced founder-engineers such as Freweini Mebrahtu.

facts.d: Authorized in 1876 under the Morrill Act framework; eight students enrolled at Alta Vista Agricultural College in March 1878.

facts.t: Renamed Prairie View A&M University in 1973.
facts.d: Earlier names include Prairie View State Normal & Industrial College and Prairie View A&M College of Texas.
Retired Lt. Gen. Julius Becton (1989–1994) and former Brown University president Ruth Simmons (2017–2023) both led the school.

sources.label: Handbook of Texas — Prairie View A&M University

name: Texas Southern University
description: Begun in 1927 as Houston Colored Junior College holding evening classes at Jack Yates High School, the school became Houston College for Negroes and was taken over by the state in 1947 as Texas State University for Negroes — a response to Heman Sweatt's lawsuit against the University of Texas law school. It is home to the Thurgood Marshall School of Law and the Jesse H. Jones School of Business, and its alumni include Barbara Jordan, Mickey Leland, oil executive Kase Lawal and investment manager Gerald B. Smith.

facts.d: In 1947, amid Sweatt v. Painter, the Texas Legislature passed Senate Bill 140 creating Texas State University for Negroes and took over Houston College for Negroes as its base.
Hugh Roy Cullen donated the current campus site.
The Jesse H. Jones School of Business hosts the Gerald B. Smith Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation, endowed by alumnus Gerald B. Smith.

sources.label: Texas Southern University — Jesse H. Jones School of Business alumni

name: Huston–Tillotson University
affiliation: United Methodist Church; United Church of Christ
description: Austin's oldest institution of higher learning, Huston–Tillotson was formed on October 24, 1952 by the merger of Tillotson College (an American Missionary Association school) and Samuel Huston College (a Methodist Episcopal school). It became a university in 2005. Its alumni include U.S. Treasurer Azie Taylor Morton.

facts.d: Tillotson College and Samuel Huston College merged to form Huston–Tillotson College; it became Huston–Tillotson University on February 28, 2005.
Before joining the Kansas City Monarchs, Jackie Robinson served as athletic director at Samuel Huston College and coached its 1944–45 basketball team.
Azie Taylor Morton (B.S. 1956) became the only African American to serve as Treasurer of the United States.

name: Samuel Huston College
fate: Merged with Tillotson College in 1952 to form Huston–Tillotson College.
description: Samuel Huston College grew out of an 1876 Methodist Episcopal conference and was developed under an 1883 agreement with the Freedmen's Aid Society; it was named for Iowa donor Samuel Huston. Jackie Robinson worked there as athletic director and basketball coach in 1944–45 before his professional baseball career.

facts.d: Named for Samuel Huston of Marengo, Iowa.
Robinson took the athletic director job at the invitation of college president Rev. Karl Downs.

connections.label: founded via Methodist Episcopal conference / Freedmen's Aid Society

name: Tillotson College
fate: Merged with Samuel Huston College in 1952 to form Huston–Tillotson College.
description: Chartered in 1877 by the American Missionary Association and named for Congregational minister George Jeffrey Tillotson, the school opened on January 17, 1881. It operated as a women's college from 1926 to 1935 before merging with Samuel Huston College in 1952.

facts.d: Tillotson Collegiate and Normal Institute opened January 17, 1881 after its 1877 charter.
It was a women's college from 1926 to 1935.

name: Paul Quinn College
formerNames: Connectional School for the Education of Negro Youth
description: Founded in Austin in 1872 by AME preachers, the school moved to Waco in 1877 and was chartered as Paul Quinn College in 1881. In 1990 it moved to Dallas onto the former Bishop College campus, acquired from businessman Comer Cottrell. Under president Michael Sorrell it became the nation's first urban work college and turned its football field into the WE over ME Farm with PepsiCo.

facts.t: Early HBCU west of the Mississippi.
facts.d: AME preachers founded it in Austin on April 4, 1872; it is described as the first HBCU established west of the Mississippi River.
Relocated to southeast Dallas in 1990 on the former Bishop College grounds.
Sorrell ended football in 2007; the WE over ME Farm, created with PepsiCo, was dedicated in 2010.
SACS moved against its accreditation in 2009; the college joined TRACS in 2011.

sources.label: Handbook of Texas — Bishop College (Paul Quinn occupies campus)

name: Wiley University
description: Founded in 1873 in Marshall by the Freedmen's Aid Society of the Methodist Episcopal Church and credited to Bishop Isaac Wiley, it is one of the oldest Black colleges west of the Mississippi. Melvin B. Tolson's debate teams — dramatized in The Great Debaters — beat national champion USC in 1935. Alumni include CORE co-founder James Farmer, Heman Sweatt, Opal Lee, and early Black bank founder H. Claude Hudson.

facts.d: Tolson's teams lost only 1 of 75 debates over 15 years; Denzel Washington gave $1 million in 2007 to restore the program.
Known as Wiley College from 1929 to 2023, it returned to the Wiley University name with new graduate programs.
Alumnus Lee Wilder Thomas struck oil in the 1920 Mexia boom and later co-built Simmons Royalty Co. in Oklahoma.

connections.label: founded by Freedmen's Aid Society of the M.E. Church

name: Jarvis Christian University
description: Planned by the Negro Disciples of Christ of Texas, the school was built on 456 acres donated by Major James Jones Jarvis and Ida Van Zandt Jarvis to the Christian Women's Board of Missions, on condition it remain a school for Black students. Instruction began in 1913. It is the only surviving HBCU of the twelve founded by the Disciples of Christ.

facts.d: The Jarvises donated 456 acres to the Christian Women's Board of Missions.

facts.t: Last of the Disciples' Black colleges.
facts.d: Only HBCU remaining of the twelve founded by the Disciples of Christ.
Renamed from Jarvis Christian College and added graduate programs in 2023.

name: Texas College
description: Founded January 9, 1894 in Tyler by ministers of the Colored (now Christian) Methodist Episcopal Church to serve Black students excluded from Texas' segregated universities. Briefly called Phillips University (1909–1912). Alumna Mildred Fay Jefferson became the first Black woman to graduate from Harvard Medical School.

facts.d: Established by a group of CME ministers in 1894.
Named for Bishop Henry Phillips 1909–1912 before becoming Texas College.
The D.R. Glass Library (1948) is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Southwestern Christian College
description: Founded in Fort Worth in 1948 as Southern Bible Institute by educator-minister G. P. Bowser, the school moved to Terrell in 1949 onto the former Texas Military College campus. Jack Evans Sr., its first Black president, led it for fifty years (1967–2017).

facts.d: Moved to Terrell in fall 1949 after buying the closed Texas Military College campus.
Jack Evans Sr. served 1967–2017.
SACS accreditation to award associate and bachelor's degrees.

name: St. Philip's College
affiliation: Founded by Episcopal Diocese of West Texas; now Alamo Colleges District
formerNames: St. Philip's Normal and Industrial School
description: Founded March 1, 1898 by Episcopal Bishop James Steptoe Johnston as a weekend sewing class for six Black girls, St. Philip's grew under Artemisia Bowden — administrator for 52 years — into a high school and junior college. It joined San Antonio's public junior college system in 1942 and is the westernmost HBCU in the United States.

facts.d: Began with missionary Alice G. Cowan teaching six girls.
Daughter of a formerly enslaved man, she led the school from 1902 for 52 years.
Public historically Black community college on San Antonio's East Side.

connections.label: founded by Episcopal Bishop of West Texas

name: Bishop College
fate: Lost SACS accreditation in December 1986 under federal debt and falling enrollment, filed Chapter 11 in 1987 and closed in 1988; Paul Quinn College later took over the campus.
description: Founded in Marshall in 1881 by the Baptist Home Mission Society and named for Nathan Bishop, the college moved to South Dallas in 1961 and became a major training ground for Black Baptist preachers. Alumni include publishing-and-banking pioneer R. H. Boyd, insurance and funeral magnate Mack H. Hannah Jr., novelist-publisher Sutton E. Griggs and Dallas pastor Frederick Haynes III.

facts.d: Relocated from Marshall to a new South Dallas campus.
SACS revoked accreditation in Dec. 1986, cutting off federal programs and UNCF funds; bankruptcy failed and the college closed in 1988.
R. H. Boyd built the National Baptist Publishing Board and a Nashville bank; Mack H. Hannah Jr. became perhaps the wealthiest Black Texan of his era.

connections.label: campus taken over by Paul Quinn, 1990

name: Mary Allen College
kind: Private HBCU · Women's seminary / junior college
affiliation: Presbyterian Board of Missions for Freedmen; later General Missionary Baptist Convention of Texas
fate: Closed in 1943 when Presbyterian funding ended, revived in 1944 under Black Baptist ownership, and finally closed after operating as a junior college until 1977.
description: Rooted in Rev. Samuel Fisher Tenney's 1871 Crockett Presbyterian Sabbath School, Mary Allen opened in 1886 as a seminary for Black women, named for Mary Esther Allen of the Board of Missions for Freedmen's Women's Executive Committee. It educated thousands of Black women and later men for nearly nine decades.

facts.d: Mary Esther Allen chaired the Women's Executive Committee of the Board of Missions for Freedmen from 1884.
After a 1943 closure, the General Missionary Baptist Convention of Texas owned and ran it from 1944.

sources.label: Amistad Research Center — Mary Allen College records

connections.label: operated by Texas Black Baptist convention from 1944

name: Butler College
fate: Closed in summer 1972 after enrollment fell to 58 students in 1968; it never achieved four-year accreditation.
description: Founded in 1905 by the East Texas Baptist Association as Texas Baptist Academy, the coeducational school was renamed Butler College in 1924 for its president C. M. Butler. The Texas Baptist Convention helped operate it from 1932.

facts.d: Became Butler College in 1924, honoring C. M. Butler.
Fell to 58 students by 1968; closed 1972.

connections.label: founded by East Texas Baptist Association

name: Guadalupe College
formerNames: College of the Guadalupe Baptist Association
fate: Reverted to junior-college status in 1931; a fire destroyed its main building on February 9, 1936 and efforts to restore it failed.
description: Founded in 1884 by the Guadalupe Baptist Association of Black congregations, it was the only Black Baptist institution of higher learning in South Texas. Philanthropist George W. Brackenridge funded buildings and land, and enrollment peaked above 450 in 1907.

facts.d: The only Black Baptist institution of higher learning in South Texas.
The main building burned in 1936.

name: Conroe College
kind: Private HBCU · Normal & industrial / Bible college
affiliation: American Baptist Convention of Texas (Black Baptist)
fate: Declined through financial mismanagement and competition and closed in 2011; the site was sold in 2014 and preservationists are working to save the building.
description: Opened in April 1903 by Dr. Jimmie Johnson and his wife Chaney, who sold their own farm to fund a school for African Americans less than 40 years after the Civil War. Its religious program was funded by the Houston-based American Baptist Convention of Texas.

facts.d: The Johnsons funded the school with proceeds from their farm.
A nonprofit is working to restore the deteriorating building.

sources.label: Houston Landing — Nonprofit works to restore historic Conroe College

connections.label: supported by American Baptist Convention of Texas

name: Southern University and A&M College
affiliation: State of Louisiana (Southern University System); 1890 land-grant
description: Chartered by the Louisiana General Assembly in 1880 in New Orleans and opened in 1881 with 12 students, Southern became the state's Black land-grant college in 1890 and moved to Scotlandville above Baton Rouge in 1914. It is the flagship of the only HBCU system in the U.S. Alumni include Zenith Bank founder Jim Ovia, music executive Randy Jackson and NASA engineer-turned-founder Morgan Watson.

facts.d: Early classes met in the former Israel Sinai Temple on Calliope Street, New Orleans.
Relocated to Scott's Bluff in Scotlandville.
A 1974 special legislative session created the Southern University System.

name: Southern University at New Orleans
description: Created by Act 28 of a 1956 extraordinary legislative session as a branch of Southern University, SUNO opened in Pontchartrain Park in 1959 and became a center of student civil-rights activism, home to CORE leader Oretha Castle Haley. All 11 buildings were damaged by Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005.

facts.d: Established September 4, 1956; opened September 21, 1959.
All 11 Park Campus buildings were damaged in 2005.
Only Louisiana institution offering an advanced degree in museum studies.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Southern University at New Orleans

name: Southern University at Shreveport
description: Southern University at Shreveport opened September 19, 1967 as a junior college of the Southern University System, offering associate degrees, technical diplomas and certificates in allied health, business and STEM to northwest Louisiana.

facts.d: Instruction began September 19, 1967.
Divisions in Allied Health & Nursing and in Business, Science, Technology, Engineering and Math.

name: Grambling State University
affiliation: State of Louisiana (University of Louisiana System)
formerNames: North Louisiana Agricultural and Industrial School
Louisiana Negro Normal and Industrial Institute
description: Opened November 1, 1901 under founder Charles P. Adams as the Colored Industrial and Agricultural School, Grambling became nationally famous through coach Eddie Robinson's 57-year football dynasty. Its alumni run from Packers great-turned-broadcasting owner Willie Davis to music executive Tina Davis, CPA firm leader Wayne McConnell and rapper-entrepreneur E-40.

facts.d: Robinson coached football 1941–1997 and won 408 games.
Hall of Famers include Willie Davis, Buck Buchanan, Willie Brown and Charlie Joiner; Doug Williams was Super Bowl XXII MVP.
Earned university status when graduate education programs were added.

name: Dillard University
affiliation: United Methodist Church; United Church of Christ
description: Chartered June 6, 1930 through the union of Straight College (American Missionary Association) and New Orleans University (Methodist Freedmen's Aid Society), Dillard carries a lineage back to 1868–69. Graduates include Brown University president Ruth Simmons, corporate executive Joyce Roché and musician-label founder Harold Battiste.

facts.t: A merger of two Reconstruction schools.
facts.d: Straight College and New Orleans University jointly chartered Dillard in 1930.
P.B.S. Pinchback and Louis A. Martinet, organizer of the Plessy challenge, studied law at Straight.
Joyce Roché ('70) became president of Carson Inc. and served on the AT&T board.

connections.label: via New Orleans University (Freedmen's Aid Society)

name: Straight University
fate: Renamed Straight College in 1915 and merged with New Orleans University in 1930 to form Dillard University.
description: Founded by the American Missionary Association in 1868–69, Straight ran a law department that trained Reconstruction-era leaders including Governor P.B.S. Pinchback and Louis A. Martinet, publisher of The Crusader and organizer of the Comité des Citoyens behind Plessy v. Ferguson. Businessman Walter L. Cohen, founder of People's Life Insurance, also studied there.

facts.d: Martinet earned his law degree in 1876; Pinchback graduated in 1885.
Merged into Dillard in 1930.

sources.label: Dillard University — Distinguished alumni (Straight College entries)

name: New Orleans University
fate: Merged with Straight College in 1930 to form Dillard University.
description: Established July 8, 1868 as Union Normal School by the Methodist Freedmen's Aid Society, it grew into New Orleans University, whose Flint Medical College (closed 1911) gave rise to Flint-Goodridge Hospital. It merged with Straight College in 1930 to form Dillard.

facts.d: Flint Medical College closed in 1911; Flint-Goodridge Hospital continued nurse training.
Alumnus John W. E. Bowen Sr. (1878) was among the first African Americans to earn a Ph.D.

name: Xavier University of Louisiana
affiliation: Catholic Church (Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament)
formerNames: Xavier University Preparatory School (1915 high school)
description: The only historically Black Catholic university in the U.S., Xavier was founded by St. Katharine Drexel and the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament (high school 1915, college 1925). Led for 47 years by alumnus Norman C. Francis, it is a leading producer of Black pharmacists and medical school applicants. Business alumni include Harold Doley, the first Black individual to buy a New York Stock Exchange seat.

facts.d: St. Katharine Drexel founded it through the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament.
Its College of Pharmacy trained entrepreneurs such as Lexington's Zirl Palmer, first Black Rexall franchise owner.
Alumnus Norman C. Francis was president 1968–2015.

connections.label: founded by St. Katharine Drexel & Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament

name: Leland College
affiliation: Baptist (Christian college founded by Holbrook Chamberlain)
fate: After a 1915 hurricane wrecked University Hall the New Orleans campus was sold; it reopened near Baker in 1923 but, never accredited and short of funds, closed in 1960.
description: Founded in 1870 by Brooklyn philanthropist Holbrook Chamberlain on St. Charles Avenue in New Orleans, Leland admitted students regardless of race. Its most famous graduate, Eddie Robinson (1941), became Grambling's legendary football coach.

facts.d: Original campus sat across from Audubon Park.
Robinson earned his bachelor's degree at Leland in 1941.

name: Coleman College
affiliation: Black Baptist (Springfield Baptist Association; American Baptist Home Mission Societies funding)
fate: Crippled by a 1926 fire and founder Oliver Coleman's 1927 death, the Gibsland school closed (dates given as 1937 or 1944), moved to Shreveport as a Bible college and faded by the mid-1950s.
description: Begun in 1887 by Oliver Lewis Coleman with eight students at Palestine Baptist Church in Gibsland, Coleman College is described as the first Black institution of higher learning in North Louisiana. Local farmers donated crops and lumber; it was Grambling's chief early athletic rival.

facts.d: Often called the first college for African Americans in North Louisiana.
The campus became Gibsland-Coleman High School; a marker was unveiled in 2014.

connections.label: supported by local Black Baptist association

name: Luther College (New Orleans)
kind: Private HBCU · Lutheran normal school & seminary
affiliation: Evangelical Lutheran Synodical Conference (Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod)
fate: The Synodical Conference closed it in 1925 (some sources say 1932), citing the failed seminary and high building costs; funds went to Alabama Lutheran College in Selma.
description: Founded in 1903 by the Evangelical Lutheran Synodical Conference as a secondary school, normal school and seminary for African Americans, Luther College was the sister school of Immanuel Lutheran College in North Carolina.

facts.d: The seminary closed in 1910 after graduating one student.
Resources were diverted to Alabama Lutheran College (now Concordia College Alabama).

name: Kase Lukman Lawal
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in chemistry from Texas Southern University in 1976, then an MBA from Prairie View A&M University in 1978 — a rare double-HBCU path into the energy business.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Ibadan, Nigeria, he came to Texas for university and stayed in Houston.
breakthrough: Built CAMAC (led as CEO and president from 1986) into an energy group with Nigerian oil interests, and served as chairman of Allied Energy (from 1991) and chairman-CEO of NYSE-listed Erin Energy Corporation.
legacy: A long-serving commissioner and vice chairman of the Port of Houston Authority, he became one of the most prominent African-born business leaders in Texas.

breakthroughDetail.d: CEO and president of CAMAC Holdings from 1986.
Chairman and CEO of Erin Energy Corporation (formerly CAMAC Energy).
Commissioner from 2000 and later vice chairman of the Port of Houston Authority.

legacyDetail.d: Holds degrees from both Texas Southern and Prairie View A&M.
His companies linked Houston capital and expertise with Nigerian upstream assets.

name: Gerald B. Smith
hbcuStory: Earned a BBA in finance from Texas Southern University, which later gave him an honorary doctorate; he chairs the TSU Foundation and endowed TSU's Gerald B. Smith Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation.
humbleBeginnings: A Houston finance professional who built his firm in a field where Black-owned managers were rare.
breakthrough: Founded and leads Smith Graham & Co., a Houston investment management firm, as chairman and CEO.
legacy: Sits on the boards of New York Life Insurance and the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas; inducted into the Texas Business Hall of Fame in 2021, the only person of color in that class.

breakthroughDetail.d: Chairman and CEO of the Houston investment management firm.
Inducted in 2021.
Director of New York Life Insurance and the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas.

legacyDetail.d: Chairs the TSU Foundation and created the Gerald B. Smith Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation.
Houston proclaimed a Gerald B. Smith and Anita Webber Smith Day for the couple's philanthropy.

sources.label: InnovationMap — Gerald Smith, Texas Business Hall of Fame
CultureMap Houston — Texas Business Hall of Fame

name: Michael Strahan
wealthNote: Estimate based on a 15-year NFL career and a long-running network TV contract; no audited figure is published.
hbcuStory: Played at Texas Southern University (1989–1992), where his pass-rush records got him drafted by the New York Giants; he was inducted into the Black College Football Hall of Fame in 2014.
humbleBeginnings: Raised partly in Germany as the son of an Army major, he arrived at TSU largely unrecruited.
breakthrough: After a Hall of Fame NFL career he moved into television — co-host of Live! and then Good Morning America — and built a business around his brand, including a menswear line launched with JCPenney in 2015 and his SMAC Entertainment company.
legacy: Became one of the most recognizable HBCU alumni in media, flying to space on Blue Origin in 2021.

breakthroughDetail.d: Drafted after a record-setting TSU career.
Full-time Good Morning America co-host from 2016.
Men's clothing line launched exclusively with JCPenney on September 8, 2015.

legacyDetail.d: Co-founded SMAC Entertainment to manage talent and brand deals.

sources.label: USA Today — Strahan wants to dress you (2015)

name: Megan Thee Stallion
wealthNote: Estimate from multi-platinum recording and endorsement career; no audited figure.
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in health administration from Texas Southern University on December 11, 2021, finishing her degree while already a Grammy-winning star.
humbleBeginnings: Born Megan Pete in Houston, she studied while freestyling online, building a following before signing a record deal.
breakthrough: Broke out with chart hits and Grammy wins, trademarked “hot girl summer” in 2019, and after leaving her label launched her own Hot Girl Productions in 2023.
legacy: Founded the Pete and Thomas Foundation in 2022 for education, housing and health in Houston, and extended her brand into consumer products such as a fragrance with Coty.

breakthroughDetail.d: Completed her health administration degree in December 2021.
Founded Hot Girl Productions after her 1501 Certified Entertainment dispute ended in 2023.
Registered “hot girl summer” as a trademark in 2019.

legacyDetail.d: Pete and Thomas Foundation launched February 15, 2022.

sources.label: Texas Southern University — notable alumni (Transfer Connect)

name: Vivian Stephens
hbcuStory: Graduated from Texas Southern University in 1955 with a degree in home economics, clothing and textiles.
humbleBeginnings: A Houston native who entered New York publishing as one of very few Black editors in mass-market fiction.
breakthrough: At Dell she rose to editor-in-chief of Candlelight Romance and created the Candlelight Ecstasy line (1980); at Harlequin she launched the Harlequin American line (1983).
legacy: Credited as founder of Romance Writers of America (organized in Houston in 1980), and later became a literary agent, representing Beverly Jenkins.

breakthroughDetail.d: Candlelight Ecstasy launched in 1980.
Launched the line, which debuted in 1983.

legacyDetail.d: Romance Writers of America grew from a December 1980 meeting in Houston.

sources.label: Bowling Green State University — Vivian Stephens collection

name: Percy Sutton
hbcuStory: Attended Prairie View A&M (then Prairie View State Normal & Industrial College), Tuskegee and Hampton without taking a degree before Brooklyn Law School (LL.B. 1950).
humbleBeginnings: Youngest of 15 children of a San Antonio educator-farmer; his brother G. J. Sutton also became a businessman and legislator.
breakthrough: In 1971 he co-founded Inner City Broadcasting Corporation, which bought WLIB-AM and WBLS-FM — making WBLS New York's first African-American-owned radio station.
legacy: Also invested in the New York Amsterdam News, bought and revived Harlem's Apollo Theater and produced It's Showtime at the Apollo; he was Manhattan Borough President and Malcolm X's attorney.

breakthroughDetail.d: Co-founded in 1971; acquired WLIB and WBLS.
Invested in and revived the Harlem landmark; It's Showtime at the Apollo premiered in 1987.
Manhattan Borough President and a member of Harlem's ‘Gang of Four’.

legacyDetail.d: Built one of the most important Black-owned broadcast groups in the country.

name: Calvin Rolark
hbcuStory: Earned a bachelor's degree in business administration from Prairie View College (now Prairie View A&M); he also attended Tennessee State, Michigan State and Cornell.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Texarkana, Texas, he worked as an editor of the Memphis World in the 1940s before moving to Washington.
breakthrough: Founded The Washington Informer newspaper in 1962, giving D.C.'s Black community its own weekly voice.
legacy: Founded the United Black Fund in 1969 as a Black-led alternative to United Way; the Informer remains in his family's hands.

breakthroughDetail.d: Founded 1962.
Founded 1969 to fund Black and Latino community organizations.

legacyDetail.d: The Informer continued under his family after his 1994 death.

sources.label: Washington Post — Crusading publisher Calvin Rolark dies (1994)

name: Je'Caryous Johnson
hbcuStory: Attended Prairie View A&M University before finishing a BFA at the University of Houston.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Houston, he started a production company with his uncle Gary Guidry.
breakthrough: Built I'm Ready Productions — later Je'Caryous Johnson Entertainment — into a leading producer of touring Black stage plays, from Men Cry in the Dark (2002) to New Jack City: Live on Stage.
legacy: Develops stage adaptations of Black film and music catalogs, a niche business model in live entertainment.

breakthroughDetail.d: Productions include The Maintenance Man, Two Can Play That Game and Set It Off: Live on Stage.
Honored at the NAACP Theatre Awards (2007).

legacyDetail.d: Turning ’90s Black films into live shows created a repeatable product line.

name: DJ Premier
hbcuStory: Attended Prairie View A&M University, where he was the campus DJ and occasionally performed with the Marching Storm band.
humbleBeginnings: Born Christopher Martin in Houston's Fifth Ward.
breakthrough: As half of Gang Starr and producer for Nas, Jay-Z and The Notorious B.I.G., he became one of hip-hop's most influential producers.
legacy: Founded his own label, Year Round Records, in 2010.

breakthroughDetail.d: Co-led the influential duo with Guru.
Year Round Records founded 2010.

legacyDetail.d: His production catalog underpins a long-running royalty business.

sources.label: Red Bull Music Academy — DJ Premier lecture

name: Freweini Mebrahtu
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in chemical engineering from Prairie View A&M University in 1992.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Ethiopia's Tigray region, where lack of menstrual products kept girls out of school.
breakthrough: Founded Mariam Seba Sanitary Products Factory in 2009, manufacturing reusable sanitary pads sold in ‘dignity packs’ and employing local women.
legacy: Named 2019 CNN Hero of the Year for keeping girls in school through her factory and education work.

breakthroughDetail.d: Mariam Seba Sanitary Products Factory, founded 2009.

legacyDetail.d: Employs dozens of local women.

sources.label: CNN — 2019 CNN Hero of the Year

name: Willie Davis
wealthNote: Estimate based on ownership of a multi-station radio group and decades of public-company board fees; no published figure.
hbcuStory: Played football at Grambling (1954–1957) under coach Eddie Robinson before the NFL; later earned an MBA from the University of Chicago (1968).
humbleBeginnings: Born in Lisbon, Louisiana, and raised in Texarkana, Arkansas, by a single mother.
breakthrough: After a Hall of Fame career with the Green Bay Packers he became president of All-Pro Broadcasting (from 1976), owning radio stations in Los Angeles, Milwaukee and elsewhere.
legacy: Became one of the most sought-after Black corporate directors of his era — Sara Lee, MGM, Manpower, Dow Chemical, Johnson Controls, Kmart and others.

breakthroughDetail.d: President from 1976; stations included KHTI, WLUM-FM and WZTI.
University of Chicago MBA, 1968.
Directorships at Sara Lee (1983–2020), MGM (1999–2020), Manpower (2001–2020) and more.

legacyDetail.d: Long tenures on Fortune 500 boards opened doors for later Black directors.

sources.label: Investor's Business Daily — It's been all business for Packers great Willie Davis
Packers.com — Packers legend Willie Davis dies at 85

name: E-40
wealthNote: Estimate from three decades of independent record sales plus beverage brands; no published audited figure.
hbcuStory: Enrolled at Grambling State University in 1986 with his cousin and attended for one year.
humbleBeginnings: Born Earl Stevens in Vallejo, California, he sold tapes out of car trunks with his family.
breakthrough: Founded the independent label Sick Wid It Records (1989) and later built a beverage portfolio — Earl Stevens Selections wines, the Sluricane premixed cocktail and E-40 malt liquor.
legacy: Diversified into franchises (a Fatburger with Chester McGlockton) and early-stage tech investments such as Clubhouse.

breakthroughDetail.d: Independent label founded 1989.
Earl Stevens Selections wines including ‘Function’ and ‘Mangoscato’.
Sluricane (2014) and E-40 malt liquor (2015).

legacyDetail.d: Kept masters and brands in-house rather than relying solely on major labels.

sources.label: SFGate — Bay Area rap legend E-40 finds success in wine

name: Tina Davis
hbcuStory: A Grambling State University alumna from Vallejo, California.
humbleBeginnings: Started in the music business and rose through A&R.
breakthrough: Became the first woman to head A&R at Def Jam, founded artist-management firm Phase Too (2008) — managing Chris Brown among others — and in June 2023 was named president of independent label and distributor EMPIRE.
legacy: One of the most senior women executives in independent music.

breakthroughDetail.d: First woman to head Def Jam's A&R department.
Joined 2018, SVP 2021, president June 2023.

legacyDetail.d: Founded Phase Too in 2008.

sources.label: Billboard — Tina Davis named president of EMPIRE
Variety — Empire names Tina Davis president

name: Wayne McConnell
hbcuStory: Earned his accounting degree at Grambling State University in 1972; Grambling lists him among its notable business alumni.
humbleBeginnings: Entered public accounting at a time when very few Black CPAs led firms.
breakthrough: As longtime managing partner of Houston-based McConnell & Jones LLP, he built what the firm calls the largest majority African-American-owned CPA firm in the U.S., with offices in seven cities.
legacy: Is transitioning from managing partner to chairman, handing day-to-day leadership to William A. Taylor Jr.

breakthroughDetail.d: McConnell & Jones describes itself as the largest majority African-American-owned and controlled CPA firm in the US.
Offices in Houston, Durham, Washington, Atlanta, Austin, Columbus (GA) and Dallas.
